review.notes: Built on the course: hazard vs risk, near miss, Swiss cheese, leading vs lagging, L x S rating and bands, hierarchy of controls, LOTO, TILE, forklifts, incident response, 5 Whys, LTIFR per million hours. Calculations checked. Fictional company.

content.company: Polaris Packaging (fictional), a plant making cartons on three production lines
content.briefing: Last week a glove was pulled into a roller on line 3; the operator was lucky. The plant manager wants the line safe and a report by Friday. You also handle the daily safety work on the floor.

variants.text: An operator's glove was pulled into roller 3. He pulled his hand free with no injury. How do you classify it?

choices.t: A near miss: an incident with no harm
choices.f: Correct. Near misses share causes with serious accidents. It is a free chance to fix the problem.

choices.t: Nothing to report: nobody was hurt
choices.f: Unreported near misses mean the next one may be an amputation.

choices.t: An accident: equipment was involved
choices.f: An accident causes harm. This is an incident that could have.

variants.text: A supervisor says: 'Near misses just create paperwork.' Reports have dropped to zero.

choices.t: Make reporting quick and thank every reporter
choices.f: Reports return within a month. Reporting must be easy, fast and appreciated.

choices.t: Agree, and focus only on real injuries
choices.f: Zero reports does not mean zero risk. You lose your early warning.

choices.t: Make near-miss reporting a disciplinary duty
choices.f: Required, yes, but fear of blame cuts honest reporting.

variants.text: First minutes after a worker cut his arm on a guillotine. What comes first?

choices.t: Make the area safe and give first aid
choices.f: Correct order: safe area, first aid, preserve the scene, then report.

choices.t: Interview witnesses before they forget
choices.f: People first. Evidence and interviews come after the area is safe and he is treated.

choices.t: Restart the line to keep the order on time
choices.f: Restarting destroys evidence and may hurt someone else.

variants.text: Glove pulled into roller 3. 5 Whys so far: the guard was removed, because cleaning took too long with it on. What next?

choices.t: Ask why cleaning took too long, answering with facts
choices.f: You find the guard needs 12 bolts. A hinged guard with an interlock fixes the root cause.

choices.t: Stop here: the operator broke the rule
choices.f: That blames the person and leaves the cause. Look behind the person.

choices.t: Retrain all operators on the guard rule
choices.f: Training helps, but the latent cause, a hard-to-remove guard, remains.

variants.text: Swiss cheese model: the guard was off, the supervisor knew, and cleaning targets were tight. Which are latent conditions?

choices.t: The hard-to-clean guard design and the tight targets
choices.f: Latent conditions sit in design, targets and resources. They are what managers can fix.

choices.t: The operator putting his hand near the roller
choices.f: That is an active failure at the front line.

choices.t: Only the supervisor not stopping the work
choices.f: That is one layer, but design and targets made the failure likely.

variants.text: Your report's corrective action says only: 'Operator to be more careful.' What do you change?

choices.t: Real fixes from the hierarchy, each with an owner
choices.f: Interlocked guard, cleaning procedure, check of effectiveness: real fixes with owners.

choices.t: Nothing more; the operator has agreed to it
choices.f: 'Be careful' is not a control. The same incident will happen again.

choices.t: Add a written warning to the operator's file
choices.f: Discipline does not fix the root cause, a guard that is hard to clean.

variants.text: Cleaning roller 3 with the guard off: likelihood 4, severity 4. Bands: 1-4 low, 5-9 medium, 10-16 high, 20-25 very high.

choices.t: 16: high
choices.f: Correct: 4 x 4 = 16, in the high band. Action is needed before work continues.

choices.t: 8: medium
choices.f: You added instead of multiplying. Rating = likelihood x severity.

choices.t: 20: very high
choices.f: Recheck: 4 x 4 is 16, which is high.

variants.text: After an interlocked guard is fitted, likelihood drops to 1 and severity stays 4. What is the residual risk?

choices.t: 4: low
choices.f: Correct: 1 x 4 = 4, low. The controls are enough.

choices.t: 16: unchanged
choices.f: You did not re-rate after controls. Residual risk uses the new likelihood.

choices.t: 0: risk removed
choices.f: The hazard still exists. Risk is reduced, not zero.

variants.text: Glue fumes cause headaches at line 2. Which control do you try first?

choices.t: Switch to a less hazardous water-based glue
choices.f: Substitution sits high in the hierarchy and works without relying on people.

choices.t: Give all operators respirator masks
choices.f: PPE is the last line. It fails silently if fit or use is wrong.

choices.t: Rotate operators every two hours
choices.f: An administrative control. It reduces exposure but the hazard stays.

variants.text: Operators can reach into the moving roller during work. What is the strongest practical control?

choices.t: A fixed guard with an interlock that stops the roller
choices.f: An engineering control: it protects even when someone makes a mistake.

choices.t: A sign saying 'Do not reach into the roller'
choices.f: Signs depend on attention every second. They fail.

choices.t: Cut-resistant gloves for all operators
choices.f: Gloves can be pulled in. PPE is not a fix for an entrapment hazard.

variants.text: A fitter must clear a jam inside the hydraulic press. He switched it off at the button. Is it safe?

choices.t: No: isolate every energy source, lock, bleed, then test
choices.f: Lockout-tagout. Stored hydraulic pressure can still move the press.

choices.t: Yes: the press is switched off
choices.f: Switching off is not isolation. Someone could restart it or stored energy could move it.

choices.t: Yes, if someone watches the start button
choices.f: A watcher is not a lock. One person, one lock.

variants.text: Two fitters work inside the same machine under lockout. How many locks?

choices.t: Two: each fits a personal lock and tag
choices.f: One person, one lock. Only the lock owner removes it.

choices.t: One: the senior fitter's lock covers both
choices.f: If he leaves and removes it, the other fitter is exposed.

choices.t: None if the supervisor stays nearby
choices.f: Supervision is not isolation. Locks protect each person.

variants.text: Workers lift 25 kg glue drums from the floor, twisting, in a narrow aisle. Using TILE, what is the best fix?

choices.t: A trolley and drum stand, so nobody lifts
choices.f: You change the Task and Environment, not just the person. Back complaints stop.

choices.t: Train all workers in safe lifting technique
choices.f: Useful, but the twisting and floor-level lift remain.

choices.t: Ask only the strongest workers to lift them
choices.f: Strength does not remove the hazard. Injuries still happen.

variants.text: Forklifts and pedestrians share the loading bay. There was a near miss yesterday.

choices.t: Separate them with barriers and marked walkways
choices.f: Physical separation is an engineering control. It works when people forget.

choices.t: Tell drivers to sound the horn more often
choices.f: Helpful, but people still walk into vehicle routes.

choices.t: Ask pedestrians to wear high-visibility vests
choices.f: PPE alone, when separation is possible, is the weakest choice.

variants.text: The plant had 3 lost-time injuries and 600,000 hours worked this year. What is the LTIFR?

choices.t: 5.0 per million hours
0.5 per million hours
choices.f: Check the multiplier: 3 / 600,000 x 1,000,000 = 5.0.

choices.t: 200 per million hours
choices.f: You divided the wrong way. LTIFR = injuries x 1,000,000 / hours.

variants.text: 1 lost-time injury, 250,000 hours worked. What is the LTIFR?

choices.t: 4.0 per million hours
0.4 per million hours
choices.f: The multiplier is 1,000,000. Recheck: 1,000,000 / 250,000 = 4.

choices.t: 25 per million hours
choices.f: That uses the hours wrongly. LTIFR = injuries x 1,000,000 / hours.

variants.text: The board looks only at LTIFR. You want early warning. What do you add?

choices.t: Add leading indicators such as near misses
choices.f: Leading indicators measure prevention before harm happens.

choices.t: Add more detail on each lost-time injury
choices.f: Still lagging. It measures harm after it happens.

choices.t: Add total medical costs for each quarter
choices.f: Another lagging measure. It arrives too late to prevent anything.

variants.text: Night shift skips PPE when no manager is around. What does this say, and what do you do?

choices.t: Weak culture: supervisors must lead it on every shift
choices.f: Culture is how people behave when no one is watching. Supervisors enforce and model it.

choices.t: Nothing serious, since the day shift fully complies
choices.f: Night shift is where the next injury will happen.

choices.t: Install cameras on the line to catch rule breakers
choices.f: Monitoring may help, but culture changes through leadership, not only cameras.

variants.text: A small paper fire starts in a waste bin. Which part of the fire triangle does a water extinguisher remove?

choices.t: Heat
choices.f: Water cools. Match the extinguisher to the fire class, then use PASS.

choices.t: Oxygen
choices.f: Smothering removes oxygen, as with a fire blanket or CO2.

choices.t: Fuel
choices.f: Removing fuel means taking away what burns.

variants.text: A painter must work on a roof edge with no guardrail for one hour.

choices.t: Fit temporary guardrails before work starts
choices.f: Prevent falls with guardrails first; harnesses and nets mitigate.

choices.t: Ask him to be careful and work quickly
choices.f: Speed and care do not stop a fall from height.

choices.t: Give him a harness and let him start
choices.f: Mitigation is better than nothing, but prevention comes first.
